title: The Impact of Item Flaws, Testing at Low Cognitive Level, and Low Distractor Functioning on Multiple-Choice Question Quality https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40037-015-0212-x
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 10, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton's summary covers Ali and Ruit's experimental study of medical-education multiple-choice questions, which manipulated three groups of items: one where item flaws were corrected and cognitive level raised, one where ineffective distractors were replaced, and an unchanged control group. The intervention groups showed significantly better discrimination between high- and low-performing students than the control, demonstrating that fixable, mechanical problems in item construction — not just teaching quality — can distort what an assessment actually measures. The paper catalogs common item-writing flaws (grammatical or logical cues, absolute terms, overly long correct answers, word overlap between stem and answer) that let test-wise students succeed without genuine understanding. It also argues for testing at a higher cognitive level using clinical vignettes rather than simple recall, since low-cognitive-level items are both easier to game and more prone to flaws.
points: Correcting item-writing flaws and replacing non-functioning distractors measurably improved how well questions discriminated between strong and weak students — a fixable technical problem, not a teaching problem.
Common item flaws (grammatical/logical cues, absolute terms, long correct answers, stem-answer word overlap) let 'test-wise' students succeed without real understanding.
A functioning distractor is one selected by at least 5% of students and disproportionately by lower-performing students; anything less should be revised or removed.
Testing higher-order application of knowledge via clinical vignettes, rather than simple recall, produces better and less flaw-prone items.
quotes: Researchers manipulated MCQs in three groups: one group corrected item flaws and raised the cognitive level, another replaced ineffective distractors, and a control group remained unchanged.
improvements to the MCQs led to significantly better discrimination between high- and low-performing students

Teachers should be aware of common item writing flaws that can affect the validity of scores. These flaws, which can lead to construct-irrelevant variance, include grammatical or logical cues, absolute terms, long correct answers, word repeats between the stem and the correct answer, and convergence strategies.

A functioning distractor is an incorrect option selected by at least 5% of the students and is more often selected by low-performing students. Teachers should avoid or replace non-functioning distractors to improve the discriminatory ability of the questions.
Correction of item flaws, removal or replacement of non-functioning distractors, and enhancement of tested cognitive level positively impact the discriminatory ability of multiple-choice questions

Teachers should strive to assess higher cognitive functions, such as the application of knowledge, rather than just factual recall. Using clinical vignettes can help assess a student's ability to apply knowledge.
